answer.summary: Paige Costello advises new PMs to trade the pressure to appear all-knowing for genuine curiosity and openness: ask questions, invite feedback, and be willing to say when you do not know. She says this can convey more confidence than constant assertiveness.

sections.heading: Choose inquiry over pretending to be the expert
sections.content: Trying to be “pro” too quickly or insisting you are the smartest person in the room can cut off information and useful conversation. Instead of doing discovery or drafting a spec in isolation and presenting it as final, collaborate with genuine curiosity—not just performative collaboration where you do not really want questions or feedback.

sections.heading: Ask, listen, and handle feedback thoughtfully
sections.content: Ask clarifying questions and the question behind the question. Listen to feedback, then consider whether it is something you must do, should do, or should consider. Costello notes that others may not always be right, but being present and curious lets you have a conversation that can improve the work and the relationship.

sections.heading: Show confidence through openness and preparation
sections.content: Be brave in small moments: speak before you feel fully ready, be vulnerable, and say, “I don’t know what you mean by that. Can you say that again?” Costello says this can build more trust than arriving armored with certainty. In meetings, be present rather than checking Slack, look at people and scan for questions, welcome participants, and close by asking what was missed. Build credibility by bringing insight about customers, the market, competitors, numbers, and your product; she cautions against pretending to have more experience or expertise than you do.

answer.summary: Paige’s advice is to trade the pressure to appear all-knowing for genuine curiosity: ask questions, invite feedback, and be open about what you don’t know. She says that openness can project more confidence than constant assertiveness.

sections.heading: Choose inquiry over acting like the expert
sections.content: Trying to be the smartest person in the room can put a PM in advocacy mode and cut off conversations that would make them smarter. Instead, be genuinely curious and collaborative—not just performatively open to review. Ask clarifying questions and “the question behind the question”; listen to feedback, then sort it by asking whether it’s something you must do, should do, or should consider.

sections.heading: Show confidence through openness and presence
sections.content: Paige recommends being brave in small moments: speak before you feel fully ready, be vulnerable, and say, “I don’t know what you mean by that. Can you say that again?” In meetings, be present rather than distracted by your computer, scan the room for questions, pause and welcome people, and close by asking, “Did I get all of that?” or whether anything expected was missed. She says openness conveys confidence better than being assertive and advocating all the time. To build trust without pretending to have others’ expertise, bring useful insight: learn the customer, market, competitors, numbers, and product, including by watching customers use the product firsthand.
